questions.scenario: A healthcare provider in Germany is deploying a chat model in Microsoft Foundry. Company policy states that prompts and responses must be processed only within the European Union. The provider wants to pay per token.
questions.question: Which deployment type should the provider use?

options.why: Global Standard can process requests in any Azure region, so it does not meet the EU processing requirement.
Global Batch can also process requests in any region, and it is asynchronous rather than interactive.
Correct. Data Zone Standard keeps processing within the selected data zone, such as the EU, and is billed per token.
Developer deployments are for evaluating fine-tuned models, have no SLA and process requests globally.

questions.explanation: Data Zone deployments keep processing inside a Microsoft-defined data zone (US, EU or APAC) while still using pay-per-token billing.

questions.question: A company must summarize several hundred thousand documents each week. The results are not time-sensitive, and the company wants to minimize cost. Which deployment type should the company use?

options.why: Correct. Batch deployments process files of requests asynchronously with a 24-hour target at a significantly lower price than standard deployments.
Provisioned deployments reserve capacity for steady, low-latency traffic. They are not the lowest-cost option for occasional, non-urgent jobs.
Global Standard works, but it is billed at the standard rate and is designed for real-time requests.
Developer deployments are intended for evaluating fine-tuned models, not production workloads.

questions.explanation: Batch deployments suit large, non-urgent workloads and cost about 50 percent less than standard deployments.

questions.question: A developer notices that a model returns noticeably different answers each time the same factual question is asked. The developer wants more consistent answers. What should the developer do?

options.why: A higher temperature increases randomness and makes answers vary more.
Correct. A lower temperature makes the model choose the most likely tokens, which produces more focused and repeatable answers.
A higher presence penalty encourages the model to introduce new topics, which does not improve consistency.
Max output tokens limits response length. It does not control randomness.

questions.explanation: Temperature controls randomness. Lower values give more deterministic responses.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about provisioned deployments in Microsoft Foundry are correct?

options.text: Capacity is reserved in provisioned throughput units (PTUs)
options.why: Correct. Provisioned deployments are sized and billed by PTUs.

options.text: They provide predictable latency for steady, high-volume workloads
options.why: Correct. Reserved capacity gives low latency variance.

options.text: They process requests asynchronously with a 24-hour target
options.why: That describes Batch deployments, not Provisioned deployments.

options.text: They are billed only per token with no reserved capacity
options.why: Pay-per-token billing without reserved capacity describes Standard deployments.

questions.explanation: Provisioned deployments reserve model capacity in PTUs, which suits steady traffic that needs consistent latency.

questions.question: You need to ensure that a model never returns a response longer than approximately 200 tokens. Which parameter should you configure?

options.why: Top_p limits the set of candidate tokens to control randomness. It does not cap length.
Frequency penalty reduces repetition. It does not cap length.
Correct. Max output tokens sets the maximum number of tokens the model can generate in a response.
Temperature controls randomness, not response length.

questions.explanation: The max output tokens (max tokens) parameter sets an upper limit on the length of the generated response.
